phase_title: Villas and country cottages on the slope
name_fr: Villa et maison de campagne pittoresque
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Free-standing houses in their own grounds along the chemin de la Côte-Saint-Antoine (23.E.14) and at Rosemount (23.E.8), the 'berceau de Westmount' of about 1874, at low density and with deep setbacks.
blurb_en: The picturesque villas and country cottages of the slope, standing in their own grounds before the street grid reached them: Metcalfe Terrace (1840), Braemar and Riverview (1847).
origin_en: The first houses built for pleasure rather than farming on the Côte-Saint-Antoine lands, whose rural antecedent — the Maison Hurtubise of 1739, classified in 2004 — still stands on the founding road. Braemar (1847, 3219 The Boulevard) was recognised in 1984.

phase_title: Greystone rows and the first Queen Anne houses
name_fr: Maison en rangée en pierre grise
source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sectors 23.E.24, 23.E.22, 23.E.33
siting_landscape: The flat lower town; buildings aligned to the street with shallow or no front garden; runs of up to eight units (sector 23.E.24, 1885–1905). | Hallowell-Weredale (23.E.33): about 240 buildings, mostly attached town houses of 1870–1914, the first Westmount project with paved rear lanes.
massing: Two to three storeys, narrow party-wall units; flat roof or false-mansard crown.
articulation: Repetitive bays; cornices; decorative wood joinery ("tarabiscotage"), polychrome and nearly intact at Place de Blenheim (23.E.31, sixteen identical façades).
materials: Le calcaire local — 'la pierre grise de Montréal' — préféré à la brique dans ce secteur (23.E.24).
blurb_en: The lower town's default building: a narrow greystone unit repeated up to eight times in a run, flat-roofed or crowned with a false mansard, its individuality carried entirely by the cornice and the painted woodwork of the entrance.
origin_en: Built 1870–1905 as Westmount urbanised the flat land below the escarpment; the same Montréal greystone that faces the Plateau's maisons urbaines, quarried from the cliff itself. Parks Canada's statement lists row houses among the components whose "diversity and integrity" make the district an exemplary Victorian and post-Victorian suburb.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: Greystone rows and the first Queen Anne houses
name_fr: Triplex en pierre grise à escalier extérieur
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Rue Saint-Antoine (23.E.34), at the northern edge of the flat lower town.
massing: Attached greystone triplexes of the 1890s reached by straight, steep exterior stairs.
materials: Montréal greystone.
blurb_en: The Montréal plex as Westmount rarely built it: three flats behind a greystone front, the upper two reached by a straight outside stair, on one street at the town's northern edge.
origin_en: The 2005 fiche is explicit that this is a borrowed form — « ce genre de construction typique de Montréal se retrouve rarement à Westmount » — which is why it is the cross-link between Westmount and the plex cities of the Plateau and Saint-Lambert.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: Greystone rows and the first Queen Anne houses
name_en: Mansard-roofed house of Second Empire influence
name_fr: Maison à mansarde d'influence Second Empire
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Wood and Elm south of Sherbrooke (23.E.24), built 1885–1905.
massing: Mansard roof with dormers.
materials: Greystone or brick; slate on the mansard.
blurb_en: The mansard-roofed house of the lower town, its dormered brisis carrying the storey that the flat-roofed row next door does without.
origin_en: The Second Empire fashion as it reached Westmount's speculative streets in the 1880s and 90s; the 2005 fiche notes that in this sector the false mansard is more common than the plain parapet as a crown.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: Greystone rows and the first Queen Anne houses
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Metcalfe and Melbourne in the Lower Westmount residences sector (23.E.21), 1880s; flat-roofed villa-type houses on Redfern.
articulation: Asymmetry, turrets and wraparound porches.
materials: Red brick and stone with wood trim.
blurb_en: The elaborate Victorian of the lower town: asymmetrical, turreted, wrapped in a porch, and built for the first generation of Westmount's professional class.
origin_en: Built through the 1880s on Metcalfe and Melbourne as the village became a town; the same late-Victorian eclecticism that produced Saint-Lambert's Queen Anne houses in the same decade.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: Greystone rows and the first Queen Anne houses
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
articulation: Round arches and squat columns.
materials: Heavy rusticated stone.
blurb_en: The heavy stone house of the 1890s: rusticated walls, round arches over the door, squat columns carrying the porch.
origin_en: Richardsonian Romanesque as it arrived in Montréal's western suburbs at the end of the nineteenth century; the 2005 evaluation names it among the district's idioms without tying it to a single sector.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: The summit opens — eclectic prestige and brick semi-detached
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: South of The Boulevard on the west of the mountain (23.E.3), on streets traced between 1906 and 1930; avenue Grosvenor (23.E.28), where many of the two-storey brick rows are duplexes.
massing: Two storeys, paired, under a flat roof.
materials: Red or buff brick.
blurb_en: The paired brick house of the early twentieth century, flat-roofed and plain, filling the streets west of the mountain as the summit above filled with châteaux.
origin_en: Built as Westmount's middle slope was subdivided between 1906 and 1930; the 2005 fiche contrasts these flat-roofed brick pairs south of The Boulevard with the stone-and-stucco pitched-roof houses to the north.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

phase_title: The summit opens — eclectic prestige and brick semi-detached
name_en: Eclectic prestige house of the summit
source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
style_label: Georgian Revival / Colonial Revival (New England / Cape Cod) / Beaux-Arts / Château style / Edwardian classical
siting_landscape: The summit and the eastern south slope (23.E.1), largely vacant until 1895 and built up between 1900 and 1930; the steep south-west slope of Sunnyside and chemin Edgehill (23.E.2).
materials: Limestone, buff brick, terracotta and copper.
blurb_en: The summit houses — « de véritables châteaux » in the 2005 fiche's phrase — built between 1900 and 1930 for the view, in whichever historicist idiom the owner and architect preferred.
origin_en: The summit opened after The Boulevard was linked to Montréal in 1895. Stonehurst and Stonehenge (4200 and 4250 Sherbrooke West, 1928, J. J. Perrault and J. R. Gadbois) are the type's best-known pair.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Around Place Park (23.E.35), where interwar neo-Tudor apartment ensembles stand; Saint-Sulpice and Ramezay (23.E.9), stone residences of about 1930 on gently curved garden-city streets.
materials: Stone, stucco and half-timbering; slate.
blurb_en: The interwar idiom Westmount chose for itself, domestic and civic alike — the City Hall of 1922 and Victoria Hall are Tudor Revival, and so are the houses around them.
origin_en: Neo-Tudor was the dominant interwar manner across anglophone Montréal; Westmount applied it to public buildings as well as houses, which is why the type reads as the town's signature. The same idiom names Mount Royal's English Manor House and Saint-Lambert's King Cottage.
photo_credit: 66 chemin Saint-Sulpice, Westmount (sector 23.E.9), built 1927. Photograph © Jeangagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (File:66, chemin Saint-Sulpice.JPG).

source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Douglas and Grenville (23.E.4), curvilinear streets laid out by the architect W. S. Wright on garden-city principles, mid-1920s; Priests' Farm (23.E.11), built 1926–1930 by L. E. Schlemm to plans by Shorey and Ritchie, « l'un des premiers projets canadiens à adopter les rues sinueuses ».
massing: Semi-detached houses; at Priests' Farm, flat roofs to the south and steep pitches to the north.
materials: Brick.
blurb_en: The garden-city enclaves: brick semi-detached houses on curving streets, built in the mid-1920s at Douglas and Grenville and at Priests' Farm, which straddles the Montréal boundary.
origin_en: The Garden City idea reaching Westmount a decade after it built Mount Royal, and in the same Arts and Crafts vocabulary — which is why this record and Mount Royal's Garden City House share a canonical form.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
style_label: Art Deco / Streamline Moderne / Tudor Revival
siting_landscape: Around the église Saint-Léon (23.E.22), where one of Westmount's first apartment buildings went up in 1907 on De Maisonneuve; interwar ensembles around Place Park (23.E.35), and along Sherbrooke and De Maisonneuve.
blurb_en: The « conciergerie »: the interwar apartment house that lined Sherbrooke and De Maisonneuve and made a luxurious urban way of living possible inside a suburb of houses.
origin_en: Westmount's first apartment building dates from 1907; the 2005 fiche describes the sector around Saint-Léon becoming « le centre d'un style de vie urbaine luxueuse » in the two decades that followed.
photo_credit: pending: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Westmount, Quebec — CC only

source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Westmount (2005), sector fiches; Parks Canada, Westmount District NHS Statement of Significance (2011)
siting_landscape: Sainte-Catherine and De Maisonneuve (23.E.30), on blocks of Elm and Wood cleared after the rezoning of the 1960s.
blurb_en: Westmount Square (Mies van der Rohe, 1967) and Place Alexis Nihon: the International Style arriving at the foot of the slope, on ground cleared of the greystone rows that stood there.
origin_en: The 1960s rezoning that permitted them demolished blocks on Elm and Wood — the same row-house fabric that sectors 23.E.24 and 23.E.33 protect a few streets away.
